title: The teacher's send-off
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: a promise at the start, and a send-off at the end: let your teacher be a god to you
carry: honor mother, father, teacher, guest as god
tomorrow: five years done. so where did the whole thing begin?

segments.voice: The peace chants, day eight. Yesterday, the Isha's last lines: the self is not the body, and fire asked to lead by the good path. Today, the last of these chants, a promise, and a send-off.

I'll call you back. I'll be there. I'll finish it this weekend. Promises in the future tense are easy to send and easy to forget. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens its first part with a chant full of them. When that part ends, the same chant comes back, almost word for word. Almost: the tense has changed. And just before it returns, the teacher says goodbye to his students.
screen: `I'LL CALL YOU BACK.` → `A CHANT FULL OF PROMISES.` → `A TEACHER SAYS GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: The chant is known by its first words, sham no mitrah. It asks Mitra, Varuna, Indra, Brihaspati and wide-striding Vishnu to be kind, honors Vayu, the wind, as Brahman made visible, and promises: I will speak the right. I will speak the true. Then comes the study. And at the end of that part, the teacher sends his students home. Speak the truth. Live by dharma. Don't neglect your study. And then four lines many Hindus still know by heart. Matri devo bhava: let your mother be a god to you. Pitri devo bhava: your father. Acharya devo bhava: your teacher. Atithi devo bhava: your guest. Give with faith; give with modesty. Then the chant returns, now in the past tense. I have spoken the right. I have spoken the true. That has protected me. Om, peace, peace, peace. Here's why it matters. Many Hindu families point to these lines for habits at home: children bow to parents and teachers, often touching their feet, and a guest is welcomed like a god. Many teachers read it this way: the Brahman the student studied is met again at home, in the people who raised him, taught him, and knock at his door. The promise is kept, and then the thanks.
screen: `I WILL SPEAK THE TRUE.` · `SATYAM VADA. DHARMAM CHARA.` · `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST.` · `I HAVE SPOKEN THE TRUE.` · then, large: `LET YOUR TEACHER BE A GOD TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one teacher, anyone who taught you something that stuck. If you pray, fold your hands and bow your head, the way many Hindu students greet a teacher. If you don't, simply hold their face in mind. Silently name one thing they gave you, and let each slow breath be part of that thanks.
The peace chants, and today sham no mitrah: I will speak the true at the start, I have spoken the true at the end, and between them, let your teacher be a god to you.
Hold on to it: honor mother, father, teacher, guest as god. The great sayings, done.

screen: `DAY 1776 COUNTS.` → `THE GREAT SAYINGS · 42 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE YEARS. WHERE DID IT BEGIN?`

howItsDone: Sham no mitrah is chanted at the opening of the Taittiriya Upanishad's first part (the Shiksha Valli), and its past-tense form is chanted when that part is finished. The teacher's send-off just before it (satyam vada, dharmam chara; matri devo bhava…) is widely memorized, and many Hindu children bow to or touch the feet of parents, elders and teachers.
